title: Quantum Machine Learning Technique for Insurance Claim Fraud Detection with Quantum Feature Selection
journal_or_venue: Journal of Information Systems Engineering and Management
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a quantum machine learning approach for home insurance claim fraud detection using a Quantum Support Vector Machine (QSVM) with a quantum feature selection method and implementations via IBM Qiskit. It compares QSVM to classical methods (SVM, KNN, XGBoost) on a real anonymized dataset, finding competitive accuracy (QSVM 98.3% vs classical SVM 99.0%) and highlighting the importance of feature selection and hybrid quantum/classical ensembles, with future work aimed at hardware implementation.
methodology_description: The study uses an empirical comparative experiment on a real home-insurance claims dataset to evaluate fraud detection performance of a domain-expert rule-based baseline, classical ML models (KNN, SVM, XGBoost) and a quantum-enhanced classifier (Quantum Support Vector Machine, QSVM). Input data (PII-scrubbed claims payment transactions with historical SAR filings and ~15 engineered/selected features) are normalized and scaled; a feature selection stage is applied to reduce dimensionality to fit NISQ constraints. For the QSVM the authors build a quantum kernel by applying a parameterized feature map (ZZFeatureMap / ZZMap) on a low-depth circuit, estimate the kernel on a cloud quantum platform (Qiskit / IBM Quantum), then train an SVM using that quantum kernel (identify support vectors in training) and classify test instances. The pipeline explicitly lists: normalization/scaling, feature selection, kernel estimation via quantum circuits, and execution on a cloud quantum backend. Performance is compared to classical baselines using accuracy (reported), and the paper also mentions recall and false positive rate as evaluation indicators. Experiments were performed using Qiskit and IBM Quantum resources (simulator/cloud) with low-depth ZZ feature maps to accommodate NISQ limitations. Results are reported as classification accuracies for KNN, SVM and QSVM and discussed against the rule-based benchmark.
experimental_setup: Quantum circuits implemented via Qiskit and executed on IBM Quantum cloud resources / simulators. The quantum classifier uses the ZZFeatureMap (ZZMap) with low circuit depth to build a quantum kernel. Classical classifiers (KNN, SVM, XGBoost) run as baselines. Data preprocessing (normalization/scaling, feature selection) performed prior to model training. Exact backend (specific QPU model or simulator name) and number of runs/shots are not reported explicitly.
dataset_used: Actual home insurance claims payment transactions with historical SAR filings; personally identifiable information scrubbed. Fifteen engineered/selected parameters/features (e.g., credit score, payment default history, outstanding debts, property age, days unoccupied, claims in past 3 years, claims in current term, various boolean flags around loss reporting and authorities/reports).

results_summary: The paper presents a hybrid evaluation of rule-based, classical (KNN, SVM) and quantum (QSVM with a ZZ feature map) approaches for insurance-claim fraud detection on a real but limited home-insurance dataset. Using IBM Qiskit simulations, the authors report high accuracies for all evaluated classifiers (KNN 97.3%, SVM 99.0%, QSVM 98.3%). While QSVM produced competitive results, it did not outperform classical SVM on this dataset. The study highlights the importance of feature selection for QML workflows, introduces a proposed feature-selection mechanism, and argues for the promise of QSVMs and quantum kernels in fraud detection — but empirical quantum advantage is not demonstrated in the reported experiments and results were obtained via simulation rather than on quantum hardware.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate an empirical quantum advantage. QSVM produced competitive but slightly lower accuracy (98.3%) than classical SVM (99.0%) on the tested dataset; experiments were run in simulation on a limited dataset. Authors claim potential for QML under NISQ constraints, but no measured advantage (speedup or accuracy improvement) is presented.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Use a quantum kernel (ZZFeatureMap) to compute inner products on low-depth quantum circuits and feed them to a classical SVM (QSVM) for classification (quantum-classical hybrid pipeline).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Feature selection and low-depth parameterized feature maps are explicitly used to fit NISQ constraints, arguing the approach is applicable in the near term on cloud quantum resources/simulators.

#limitation:qubit-count — The approach requires dimensionality reduction to match qubit limits; exact qubit counts were not reported and example figures imply small qubit usage (e.g., 3 qubits for 3 features).
#limitation:noise — The paper frames the method around low-depth circuits to accommodate NISQ noise, implying hardware noise is a practical limitation.
#limitation:data-encoding — The need for feature selection/dimensionality reduction highlights limits and costs of encoding real-world tabular data into quantum feature maps.

#limitation:simulation-only — Hardware/backend details (exact QPU vs simulator, shots, repetitions) are not clearly reported, leaving ambiguity about whether results derive from simulators or real QPUs.
contradictions: The empirical results show classical SVM accuracy (99.0%) exceeds QSVM accuracy (98.3%), contradicting any strong claim that the QSVM used here outperforms classical methods on this insurance-fraud dataset.

The paper emphasizes NISQ feasibility but also requires aggressive feature selection and low-depth circuits; this undercuts claims that the method readily scales to higher-dimensional, real-world problems without substantial classical pre-processing.
